name: Pine bark extract
lead: Maritime pine bark extract is a dietary supplement made from the bark of Pinus pinaster, consisting mostly of proanthocyanidins (procyanidins). Pycnogenol is a trademarked standardised version containing 70% procyanidins.[1] It is sold as an antioxidant and is included in some supplement and skincare products.

According to Wikipedia, the French researcher Jack Masquelier developed the extract after reading an account of Jacques Cartier's expedition in which Native Americans were described drinking a bark tea, and he used the name Pycnogenol in 1979.[1]

Researchers have studied the extract in conditions including asthma, ADHD, blood pressure, venous insufficiency and osteoarthritis. A Cochrane review, updated in 2020, found insufficient evidence for efficacy across these conditions.[1] No trial of its effect on facial appearance was identified in the reviewed sources.

paras: Masquelier is reported to have searched for the active substances in the tea described in Cartier's account, identified maritime pine bark as a source, and extracted its proanthocyanidins.[1]

A 2002 review described Pycnogenol as having a diverse pharmacology and discussed possible target sites.[2] Laboratory work reported that metabolites of the extract showed antioxidant activity and inhibited matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes involved in breakdown of skin collagen.[3] The extract has also been studied as a natural antioxidant in foods such as cooked beef.[4]

A 2012 Cochrane review, updated in 2020, concluded the evidence was insufficient to support use of the extract for any of the conditions studied.[1] Registered human trials have examined hypertension (UPBEAT, n=130),[5] ADHD,[6][7] lymphedema in breast-cancer survivors,[8] gingival inflammation,[9] traumatic brain injury,[10] and cognitive decline in combination with fish oil.[11] A study of a pine bark extract supplement reported changes in plasma antioxidant capacity and lipoprotein profile.[12] None of the reviewed human studies examined skin or appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: Masquelier uses the name Pycnogenol for his extract.[1]

card.summary: A polyphenol antioxidant supplement (Pycnogenol); studied for many conditions, not for appearance.
card.note: A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the conditions studied; no appearance trials found.

quick.overview:
Pine bark extract is a proanthocyanidin-rich supplement from French maritime pine, best known under the trademark Pycnogenol. It is promoted as an antioxidant.

Human trials have looked at blood pressure, ADHD and other conditions; a Cochrane review judged the evidence insufficient. No skin-appearance trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory work reports antioxidant activity and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases, which are linked to collagen breakdown.
quick.risks: Safety information was not detailed in the reviewed sources.
